record.paper_title: Open problems in membrane computing and how not to solve them
record.original_question: In converting a polynomial-time semi-uniform P-system construction into a uniform one, is the ability of the semi-uniform constructor M to generate super-polynomially many different membrane structures for inputs of the same length ever computationally useful, or can every such use be eliminated while preserving polynomial time and the recognized language? The obstacle is that a uniform machine F, given only input length n, cannot generally build a polynomial-size skeleton containing all possible structures produced by M on length-n inputs.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the framework of recognizer P systems (membrane systems) used as decision-problem solvers in polynomial time. Two standard constructor regimes are:

(a) Semi-uniform: a polynomial-time Turing machine M takes each input instance w (encoded as a string) and outputs a P system Π_w that decides whether w is in the language L; the time and size of Π_w are polynomially bounded in |w|.

(b) Uniform: a polynomial-time Turing machine F takes only the input length n (in unary) and outputs a single P system family member Π_n together with a polynomial-time encoding of inputs of length n as multisets that are placed into a designated input membrane of Π_n; Π_n then decides membership in L for any input of length n.

In a semi-uniform construction, M may produce, across the set of inputs of a fixed length n, super-polynomially many distinct underlying membrane structures (i.e., the rooted tree of nested membranes, ignoring multiset contents and rules attached to membranes can vary unboundedly with the specific instance w of length n). A natural obstruction to converting a semi-uniform construction into a uniform one is that F, given only n, cannot in polynomial time output a single fixed "skeleton" membrane structure that encompasses all the membrane structures M would generate on the various length-n inputs.

Question: Is the ability of a polynomial-time semi-uniform constructor M to produce super-polynomially many different membrane structures on inputs of the same length ever computationally essential? Equivalently, for every language L recognized in polynomial time by a semi-uniform family of recognizer P systems (in some fixed standard variant, e.g., P systems with active membranes), does there exist a polynomial-time uniform family of recognizer P systems (of the same variant) that decides L? Or are there variants of P systems for which this conversion provably fails, so that semi-uniform polynomial-time recognition is strictly more powerful than uniform polynomial-time recognition?
artifact.status_search_result: Equivalence of uniform and semi-uniform polynomial-time families has been established for several variants (e.g., P systems with elementary active membranes, with or without dissolution), and tighter uniformities (AC^0, L) have been shown to separate semi-uniform from uniform classes for some restricted systems. The general question of whether super-polynomially many membrane structures across same-length inputs is ever essential remains an active research question for the full family of variants; partial results exist but no complete classification.

status_evidence.title: The computational power of membrane systems under tight uniformity conditions
status_evidence.snippet: Introduces AC0 and L uniformities and studies semi-uniform vs uniform separations for membrane systems.
status_evidence.claim: The relationship between semi-uniform and uniform P-system families is sensitive to the uniformity condition and the variant, with some equivalences known and some separations established.

status_evidence.title: Computational complexity in P systems - Scholarpedia
status_evidence.snippet: Survey of uniform and semi-uniform recognizer P systems and their polynomial-time complexity classes.
status_evidence.claim: Equivalence of uniform and semi-uniform polynomial-time recognition is known for some P-system variants but is not established in full generality.
